title: TikTok Shop's $23 billion surge is forcing big name brands to rethink commerce - eMarketer
description:
TikTok Shop launched in the US in September 2023 as a marketplace built for the kind of products that convert on a five-second video.
Its algorithm made it a deceptively effective discovery engine, and personal accessories and household items became its top-selling categories.
By 2026, that discovery engine has scaled into something premium brands and fashion retailers can no longer ignore.
TikTok Shop also grades every seller on ship speed and defect rate through its own seller's scorecard, and a low score could get a listing buried or suspended.
The takeaway for marketers TikTok Shop does not reward brands that treat it solely as a media buy.
text:
TikTok Shop's rapid growth is attracting prestige retailers who are now making the leap onto the platform.

Sephora launched on TikTok Shop on September 19, six months after Ulta Beauty became the first specialty beauty retailer to sell on the platform, with Ralph Lauren and Olaplex opening storefronts of their own this spring.

Best Buy similarly debuted its own TikTok Shop with a selection of nearly 10,000 products well suited to social discovery, like headphones, cameras, small appliances, laptops and accessories.

TikTok Shop launched in the US in September 2023 as a marketplace built for the kind of products that convert on a five-second video. Its algorithm made it a deceptively effective discovery engine, and personal accessories and household items became its top-selling categories. By 2026, that discovery engine has scaled into something premium brands and fashion retailers can no longer ignore.

EMARKETER projects TikTok Shop's US retail ecommerce sales will reach $23.41 billion this year, a 48% jump YoY, which is enough to put it ahead of the US ecommerce businesses of Target, Costco, Best Buy, and Kroger.

It will be the fastest-growing online retailer among those we track by a wide margin for the second consecutive year, and Circana projects the platform could grow from roughly 1% of US retail sales today to 10% by 2028.

Since the consumers are there, brands are likely to follow. But another story is also emerging: TikTok Shop especially works for brands willing to rebuild things they didn't expect to touch, and to accept certain trade-offs a marketing plan doesn't usually have to make.

Commerce over content is key

The TikTok Shop launches that succeed share one thing in common, according to Dan Albert, co-founder of 456 Growth, a performance influencer marketing agency: They are led by someone who owns the commerce side of the business, not the content side. As soon as the channel requires an inventory decision or fulfillment service-level agreements (SLAs), a social media team "can't sign for any of it."

TikTok Shop also grades every seller on ship speed and defect rate through its own seller's scorecard, and a low score could get a listing buried or suspended. Ignore the seller's scorecard, Albert warns, and "you're not launching a brand, you're launching a bad review engine."

Staffing aside, two other risks are harder to fix. The first is pricing that spills outside the channel. Coupons, flash events, and affiliate commission stack into a real discount "before you've spent a dollar on media," Albert said, and once a wholesale buyer sees it cheaper on TikTok, "it's not a marketing problem, it's a channel-conflict problem."

The second risk is creative control, which loosens once any affiliate can describe a product however they want, something Albert calls "genuinely frightening" for brands used to stewarding every frame of their advertising.

The metric hiding behind the launch

Many brands are measuring the wrong thing. Mike Danford of Adverio, an omni-channel ecommerce growth and advertising agency, points to Ulta's earnings call as a case in point: "More than 100 million impressions. Not revenue."

Six months in, impressions were still the headline number rather than proof of sales. Albert goes further, warning that the first 60 to 90 days will "frequently look like cannibalization," and that brands trusting platform-reported return on ad spend are flying blind.

"Anyone claiming a clean number is selling something," Danford said.

He advised to track new-to-brand rate, branded search lift, and downstream sell-through on Amazon and in retail while measuring the channel's effect elsewhere, not just inside its own dashboard.

The takeaway for marketers

TikTok Shop does not reward brands that treat it solely as a media buy. It behaves like a marketplace with its own P&L, SKU logic, and attribution blind spots. The platform asks a premium brand to trade pricing discipline and creative control for proven acquisition reach.

Brands still treating TikTok Shop as an extension of their existing plan are the ones most likely to fund, as Albert puts it, "a very expensive way to lose money with confidence."

text:
Levi Strauss and Marks & Spencer, in partnership with global energy technology company Schneider Electric’s consulting practice SE Advisory Services, announced the launch of the Fashion Renewable Collaborative (FRC), a new initiative designed to accelerate renewable electricity adoption across global fashion supply chains, and inviting other fashion brands to join the effort.

The companies said that by establishing a shared approach to supplier engagement, the partnership aims to support renewable electricity adoption and help manufacturers understand, access and implement renewable electricity solutions at scale.

According to the companies, the launch comes as fashion brands seek new ways to translate their climate commitments into measurable emissions reductions across complex global supply chains, noting that supplier adoption of renewable electricity remains a significant challenge due to market barriers, limited resources, fragmented engagement efforts, and differing requests from multiple customers.

Textile processing, including fabric mills and dye houses, accounts for more than half of apparel industry emissions, according to the Apparel Impact Institute, making supplier adoption of renewable electricity one of the fastest and most scalable paths to progress.

Jennifer DuBuisson, Senior Director, Sustainability, Levi Strauss & Co., said:

“It’s become abundantly clear that the most effective way forward on emissions reduction is working in partnership with suppliers. Initiatives like this create better working relationships and a more effective path forward. The Fashion Renewable Collaborative enables greater support of suppliers that want to access or would like to increase use of renewable electricity but haven’t been able to so far, helping facilitate adoption while reducing unnecessary duplication.”

According to the companies, the FRC is designed to provide suppliers with tools, information and support for adopting renewable electricity, including digital education, market guidance and assistance in assessing and procuring renewable power. The initiative is built around a structured implementation model designed to help suppliers move from education to implementation through digital learning modules. Suppliers will also have access to support for renewable electricity procurement and deployment options, including power purchase agreements (PPAs), energy attribute certificates (EACs), on-site and distributed renewable generation and energy storage.

The FRC builds on existing supply chain renewable energy programs from Levi Strauss and Marks and Spencer, which have registered nearly 500 supplier facilities, the companies added.

Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability and Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at Marks & Spencer, said:

“Through our sustainability programme, Plan A, we’re committed to becoming a net zero business across our value chain by 2040, and that means working with others to make the transition to renewable electricity easier for our supply partners. Building on the work already underway through Re, our supply chain decarbonisation programme, the Fashion Renewable Collaborative will provide practical support, resources and greater access to renewable electricity, helping suppliers take action and facilitating change in the fashion supply chain.”

SE Advisory Services will serve as the program’s global implementation partner, and will provide its Resource Advisor+ for Supply Chain product to support supplier onboarding, engagement tracking, readiness assessments, and progress monitoring.

Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President, SE Advisory Services, said:

“Many fashion brands have made their individual commitments. Now the focus must be on helping suppliers deliver against them. The Fashion Renewable Collaborative is designed to provide suppliers with practical support and engagement that can help accelerate renewable electricity adoption at scale. We’re excited to support Levi Strauss & Co. and M&S, and future participating brands as they work together to drive meaningful supply chain decarbonization.”

text:
Immunovant has stopped development of IMVT-1402 in cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) after failing a midphase test, closing off one path to market for the anti-FcRn antibody.

The biotech, which is part of Roivant’s stable, compared IMVT-1402 to placebo in 57 adults with CLE. At Week 12, scores on a CLE area and severity scale were statistically no better on IMVT-1402 than on placebo, causing the trial to miss its primary endpoints.

Immunovant looked for some silver linings, flagging numerical trends favoring IMVT-1402 on multiple endpoints and evidence that patients with deeper IgG reductions from baseline were more likely to respond. But the “competitive landscape and the clinical results observed” persuaded the company to end IMVT-1402 development in CLE.

Shares in Immunovant fell 6% to $35 in premarket trading Wednesday from a Tuesday closing price of $37.29.

Guggenheim Securities analysts were braced for bad news after hearing Immunovant executives characterize the CLE trial as a “fact-finding proof-of-concept” study in a “competitive landscape.” The comments left the analysts “a bit cautious on this readout,” the team wrote in a note to investors last month.

Johnson & Johnson has shown FcRn blockers have potential in systemic lupus erythematosus, reporting a phase 2 win for Imaavy in the indication in January and powering into a pivotal program. But, while J&J, argenx and others are studying anti-FcRn molecules in a range of indications, CLE is largely the preserve of drug candidates with other mechanisms of action.

In March, Biogen reported a midphase win for its anti-BDCA2 antibody litifilimab in CLE. AstraZeneca and Germany's Merck KGaA are running phase 3 CLE trials of a type I interferon receptor inhibitor and a small-molecule inhibitor of Toll-like receptors 7 and 8, respectively (TLR7/8). Meanwhile, Beeline is preparing to advance its TLR7/8 inhibitor into phase 3.

While Immunovant backed away from a fight with those programs, the biotech continues to advance its anti-FcRn antibody in other indications. Immunovant is working on Graves’ disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and Sjogren’s disease. In a positive for those efforts, IMVT-1402 had a favorable safety and tolerability profile in the CLE trial.

text:
Microsoft $MSFT's Digital Crimes Unit seized 50 websites used to operate EvilTokens, an AI-assisted phishing service that compromised more than 12,000 email inboxes across over 10,000 organizations worldwide, the company said Tuesday. Through coordinated work with industry partners, Microsoft also took down more than 150 additional domains connected to the platform's broader infrastructure.

The Metropolitan Police Service's cybercrime team arrested two men, aged 32 and 38, on September 11 in connection with the alleged operation of EvilTokens, Microsoft said. Both have been released on bail while the investigation continues.

EvilTokens launched in February 2026 and was sold through Telegram at a $1,500 initiation fee plus a $500 monthly subscription. Paying customers received a phishing toolkit that included 44 email templates, AI-crafted lures adapted to a target's professional context, and a chatbot designed to comb through a breached inbox — surfacing payment-related threads, charting who held which roles, flagging trusted relationships, and suggesting how to execute fraud. Microsoft noted that the platform consolidated functions that had previously demanded specialist knowledge across identity exploitation, cloud environments, social engineering, and financial fraud, delivering them through one commercially packaged interface.

The platform worked by tricking victims into entering an authentication code on Microsoft 's legitimate sign-in page, a technique known as device-code phishing. Victims never handed over their passwords in the process, yet attackers gained full account access — and that foothold could survive a subsequent password change unless the underlying sessions and tokens were explicitly invalidated, Microsoft said.

Once an account was breached, EvilTokens' AI capabilities let criminals pinpoint employees in finance or executive positions, dig out conversations about wire transfers and outstanding invoices, and compose messages posing as familiar contacts to move fraudulent payments. Microsoft noted that in some intrusions, the attackers enrolled new devices on a compromised account within ten minutes of gaining entry, securing a durable foothold that outlasted token revocation alone.

Affected organizations spanned wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education, and healthcare. Victim activity was most heavily concentrated across six countries: the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, India, and France. According to Axios, Coinbase — which participated in the broader investigation — determined that EvilTokens generated roughly $1.1 million in revenue.

Health-ISAC joined Microsoft as a co-plaintiff in the civil action authorized by the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. Other partners included Cloudflare, Coinbase, OpenAI, Railway, SpyCloud, The Shadowserver Foundation, and TRM Labs. Microsoft described the action as its 40th court-authorized disruption and its first against an end-to-end AI-enabled cybercrime service.

Device-code phishing has become a recurring threat. The FBI warned about a similar service called Kali365 that also abused Microsoft 's device-code authentication flow to capture tokens and bypass multi-factor authentication without stealing passwords.

description:

Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development.

text:
The shift of the AI frontier toward more powerful, lower-cost models could pave the way for safely slowing development, experts say.

Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development. Otherwise financial incentives will be too powerful.

Driving the news: The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will be for the foreseeable future.

Their top executives have also shown unusual solidarity in expressing a desire to slow the pace of model development due to a troubling series of incidents in which rogue AI agents hacked outside companies.

Between the lines: To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable. That's because remaining at the so-called frontier of capabilities requires a treadmill of never-ending — and mind-boggling spending — to keep up.

Slowing the extent of that spending, some of which is used for the computing firepower needed to train new models, would help the companies generate better returns.

That wouldn't necessarily threaten spending on computing, data centers and infrastructure such as upgrading the electric grid, according to some economists and AI pros. Those investments will still be needed in order to service demand for AI usage that continues to skyrocket.

Catch up quick: Everybody gets a new model this week, and the one thing they all have in common is that they're cheaper than ever without forgoing top intelligence.

OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX all emphasized the relatively low costs of their new models this week, as well as their ability to outperform some of their own top systems from only a few months ago.

Chinese models including DeepSeek have done the same. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash, released earlier this month, is now number one on OpenRouter's leaderboard with a 172% spike in usage this week.

Reality check: The rationale for the price cuts also goes beyond safety.

In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token costs are fueling enough additional usage to increase overall AI spending, meaning higher profits for labs even as they cut costs.

This paradox is why the AI labs have a rich history of effectively cutting prices for models over time: it increases their customer base and their profits.

The bottom line: The race to win on AI costs could be the very thing that allows the labs to enable the slowdown they are seeking.

title: Google's Strategy With Its New Laptop Follows a Playbook Apple Wrote 12 Years Ago
description:
There’s no Google-made model, since Google hasn’t built a laptop of its own since it canceled the next Pixelbook and dissolved the team behind it in 2022.
“We want Android users to get a laptop that’s intuitive,” Alex Kuscher, who leads Google’s laptop and tablet work, said at a press conference ahead of launch.
Every feature that ties the laptop to an Android phone also gives its owner another reason to keep buying Android phones.
A familiar playbook This isn’t the first time we’ve seen a company link its products together so closely—Apple started tying its laptops to its phones 12 years ago.
Google also promises software updates for up to 10 years, which is a long time to keep someone inside its services.
text:
Google first teased the Googlebook in May, and pre-orders opened on September 21. There’s no Google-made model, since Google hasn’t built a laptop of its own since it canceled the next Pixelbook and dissolved the team behind it in 2022. Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo are building the first machines, which start at $899, run on Intel or Qualcomm chips, and reach US stores on October 4.

The Snapdragon models from Dell and HP use Qualcomm’s first-generation Snapdragon X Elite, an older chip than the Snapdragon X2 Elite that Qualcomm launched last year. The software runs on Android, with desktop pieces borrowed from ChromeOS. As John Solomon, Google’s vice president and general manager for laptops, tablets, and Android Enterprise, put it in the launch announcement, if you use an Android phone, “your laptop shouldn’t treat it like a stranger.”

Googlebook’s most distinctive features depend on the phone in your pocket, which only work if that phone runs Android. “We want Android users to get a laptop that’s intuitive,” Alex Kuscher, who leads Google’s laptop and tablet work, said at a press conference ahead of launch. Every feature that ties the laptop to an Android phone also gives its owner another reason to keep buying Android phones.

A familiar playbook

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen a company link its products together so closely—Apple started tying its laptops to its phones 12 years ago. In 2014, it introduced Continuity features, including Handoff, which lets you start something on an iPhone and finish it on a Mac, and Apple lets Mac owners make iPhone calls from their computers. Craig Federighi, Apple’s head of software engineering, described the result as something only Apple could deliver, because it made the hardware, the software, and the services.

Research firm CIRP found that 87 percent of people who bought a new iPhone in the first quarter of 2026 were upgrading from an older iPhone, while 12 percent had switched from Android. Owning more than one device from the same company makes people even less likely to leave. In 2023, Kantar found that 97 percent of iPhone owners in the U.S. and U.K. who also owned another Apple device stayed with an iPhone when they upgraded, seven percentage points higher than people who only owned the phone. For Samsung owners with a second Samsung device, the figure was 84 percent.

Google now wants to apply the same logic to Android. An Android phone owner who uses “Continue On” every day, or keeps their phone’s photos a click away on the laptop, would lose those habits by switching to an iPhone, because none of those features connect to iOS. Every Googlebook also comes with 12 months of Google AI Pro, which normally costs $19.99 a month and includes 5TB of cloud storage, along with three months of YouTube Premium and Adobe Photoshop, and a year of Nvidia’s GeForce NOW game streaming. That gives Google a year to turn buyers into paying subscribers, and a few terabytes of photos and files stored with Google is a lot to move somewhere else. Google also promises software updates for up to 10 years, which is a long time to keep someone inside its services.

text:
Young people are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence (AI) but knowing how to use AI does not automatically translate into jobs or income.

Training should extend to hands-on projects, such as internships and apprenticeships, so young people can hone their skills.

A lack of access to devices, connectivity and professional networks can prevent young people from benefiting from AI.

A particular kind of confidence comes from knowing how to use a tool without yet knowing what it's for. Ask young people whether they use artificial intelligence (AI) and many will say yes. But ask whether that skill has changed their economic prospects and the answer gets much murkier.

Goodwall's latest survey of young people captures this gap in stark numbers: 91% use AI at least weekly, 60.2% every day and among those who assessed their own ability, 97.1% describe themselves as at least somewhat confident using it for learning, creativity or work.

By any measure, the pace at which this generation has learned this technology is difficult to overstate. However, fluency and opportunity aren’t the same thing.

Why AI literacy alone does not lead to jobs or income

Knowing how to prompt a generative AI tool, produce content or develop an idea doesn’t, on its own, produce a paying client, an internship, a first job, startup capital or even the device and connectivity needed to keep building the skill in the first place.

That is where the next AI divide is emerging: between those who can learn the technology and those who have the opportunity to convert that learning into improved livelihoods. It is also the challenge at the centre of our work together at Goodwall and HP.

Through the Goodwall app and the AI to Opportunity programme, part of the NextGen AI Alliance, we’re helping young people to access future-focused skills and AI learning at no cost.

Participants can earn while they learn, access HP technology to strengthen their ability to work and build and connect with a global peer network where they can share ideas, learn from others and discover new opportunities.

We are also increasingly looking at how to support young entrepreneurs with the business skills, initial funding, networks and guidance they need to keep developing their ideas and careers.

Since November 2025, the second year of the partnership, 967,000 learners have accessed new AI skilling opportunities, while more than 130 HP devices have reached disconnected young people across more than 50 countries.

Turning AI skills into economic opportunity

Our ultimate aim is to give young people the skills and tools to turn that knowledge into economic opportunity and the appetite to do so is already there.

In Goodwall’s Career Compass research, 46.8% said they wanted to build their own venture, while another 43.7% were open to it. Yet 68.9% identified financial or family pressures as the biggest obstacle standing between them and their ambitions.

For someone expected to contribute financially to their household, for example, months of unpaid experimentation may not be possible. Another online course may add knowledge without changing their economic prospects.

For this reason, AI education must go deeper than AI literacy. Learning how AI works is the foundation. The economic value comes when someone can apply that knowledge to a real problem, completing a task more effectively for an employer, developing a service a customer will pay for, building a product, starting a venture or solving a problem in their community.

Our discussions with young people reveal how different that gap can look depending on where they live. In some communities, students are learning in environments with national AI strategies and institutions already integrating AI into education. In others, schools still lack information, communication and technology laboratories and students have little or no access to devices.

For young people in those settings, asking whether an AI course leads to employment is premature if they cannot reliably access the technology after the programme ends. Elsewhere, the infrastructure exists but the pathway into jobs where that knowledge can be readily applied is not clear.

“

The first AI divide was about who could access the technology and learn how to use it. The next will be about who gets to turn that knowledge into a livelihood.

”

What young people need to turn AI learning into earning

If the objective is inclusive economic participation, we need to start designing AI education backwards from the outcome we want. That means going beyond asking what a young person should learn to what needs to happen afterwards for that learning to improve their livelihood.

First, young people need opportunities to apply skills in real settings. Training should connect to projects, work-based challenges, internships, apprenticeships and entrepreneurial opportunities where learners can demonstrate their skills.

Second, they need people who can help them navigate the transition. Mentors, educators and industry professionals can turn an abstract skill into a clearer pathway: which capabilities employers value, how to build a portfolio, where opportunities exist and how an idea might become a viable business.

Third, credentials need to reflect demonstrated capability, rather than simply course completion. As AI skills become more widespread, employers will need better signals of whether someone can use those skills effectively and responsibly in practice.

Building pathways from AI skills to economic opportunity

This thinking is already shaping our own work together. Goodwall and HP are partners in the NextGen AI Alliance, founded by Goodwall with HP, Microsoft and Cognizant to expand access to AI education and prepare young people for the future of work.

It is one example of what closing the learning-to-earning gap can look like in practice: skills, tools and opportunities designed as parts of the same pathway.

This week during the UN General Assembly, Goodwall and HP will build on their shared focus on turning skills into tangible opportunities for young people. Across two high-level engagements, HP will bring its perspective on how technology can help demonstrate and scale youth impact, drawing on insights and stories from the HP Foundation’s work.

The discussions will centre on a common challenge: how to move beyond skilling alone and create clearer pathways into employment, economic opportunity and long-term resilience: from embedding AI literacy into national workforce systems to ensuring education and training translate into meaningful opportunities for young people in an AI-driven world.

The first AI divide was about who could access the technology and learn how to use it. The next will be about who gets to turn that knowledge into a livelihood. Closing the distance between learning and earning is how we ensure AI doesn't simply create a more technologically skilled generation, but a generation with greater economic opportunity.

text:
September 23, 2026 [Storage Terminals Magazine]- BlastOne has appointed Jay Worley as its new global chief executive officer, bringing more than three decades of experience in complex, safety-critical and asset-intensive businesses to the role.

Worley joins BlastOne from Airgas, an Air Liquide company, where he served as chief operating officer. In that position, he was responsible for safety, sales, marketing, operations and technology across more than 18,000 employees and approximately 1,400 locations in the United States and Canada.

He joined Airgas in 1993 and held a series of senior leadership positions over more than three decades, gaining experience across finance, sales, operations and business transformation. During his tenure as COO, Airgas achieved sustained growth and profitability through a combination of organic growth and mergers and acquisitions.

In his new role at BlastOne, Worley will build on the company’s existing focus on its people, safety, customer service and technological innovation. His experience across operations, commercial performance, strategy and business growth is expected to support BlastOne’s continued international expansion, as well as further investment in technology and automation.

BlastOne has developed from its origins in a backyard shed into a global provider of blasting, coating and surface preparation solutions, with operations across North America and the Asia-Pacific region.

The company’s growth has been driven by a focus on customers, safer and more productive working practices, and a culture centred on humility, agility and practical problem-solving. As Global CEO, Worley will work with the BlastOne team to build on these foundations and support the company’s continued development and expansion.

Worley has also held industry leadership positions, including serving on the Board of Directors of the Compressed Gas Association from 2021 to 2025. He served as Board Chair from 2024 to 2025, with his work including efforts to advance industry safety standards and support the development of emerging professionals.

BlastOne has also acknowledged the contribution of outgoing leader Matthew Rowland, thanking him for his leadership and wishing him well in his next role.

Pearson plc (GB0006776081) traded at 1,194 GBX on the London Stock Exchange on September 23, 2026, down 0.33 percent from the prior close. The company also announced three board appointments taking effect October 1, 2026, giving the education group a concrete governance catalyst.

Three directors join in October

According to Reuters on September 23, 2026, Michael Barkin and Vivek Sharma were appointed independent non-executive directors, while Alex Svensson joined as a non-executive director. All three appointments take effect on October 1, 2026.

The board update adds a defined governance timetable rather than a broad strategic promise. For shareholders, the relevant date is therefore October 1, 2026, when the appointments become effective and board oversight changes formally.

Inclusive Access grows 20 percent

Pearson's operating story has a measurable digital distribution element. According to Investing.com on September 22, 2026, Inclusive Access grew 20 percent in the first half of 2026 and represented 50 percent of Pearson's U.S. core courseware business.

That comparison matters because the 20 percent first-half increase is tied to a defined business period, while the 50 percent share shows the scale of the offering inside U.S. core courseware. The same report said Pearson has agreements with technology companies that lock in revenue commitments through 2030, although it did not quantify total group revenue or profit for the period.

Stock remains near 1,200 GBX

Pearson stock was quoted at 1,194 GBX on the London market on September 23, 2026, after a daily decline of 0.33 percent. The same market snapshot showed a five-day change of 0.42 percent and a year-to-date gain of 13.62 percent, placing the current quote close to the 1,200 GBX threshold.

A separate market listing showed Pearson at 1,198 GBX, up 0.50 percent, with a market capitalization of GBP 7.2 billion on September 23, 2026. The difference reflects separate market snapshots and is not used as the reference price here.

Reference price stays at 1,194 GBX

Pearson stock closed at the reference level of 1,194 GBX on the London Stock Exchange on September 23, 2026, with the daily change shown as minus 0.33 percent. The governance appointments and the 20 percent first-half Inclusive Access growth provide the two clearest dated company developments around that market level.

text:
Best Buy Canada has selected RELEX Solutions to optimise forecasting and replenishment across its retail network. It says it will deploy the company’s tech to improve inventory visibility, automate planning processes, and support omnichannel operations across stores and distribution centres.

Headquartered in Vancouver, British Columbia, Best Buy Canada operates more than 300 stores supported by two DCs and manages approximately 2.1 million SKUs.

It was looking for a solution to improve alignment between inventory and customer demand that would support driving greater efficiency across its network. RELEX’s ability to incorporate supply chain constraints into replenishment planning, optimise inventory across channels, support large scale retail operations, and automate key planning processes aligned closely with its goals.

“Accurate planning is essential to meeting customer expectations in a competitive consumer electronics market,” says Christian Trudel, VP Inventory & Merchandising Operations at Best Buy Canada. “RELEX gives us the tools to improve planning efficiency that supports delivering a better experience for our customers across Canada.”

“As retail operations become increasingly connected across stores, distribution centres, and digital channels, planning teams need tools that help them respond quickly and confidently,” says Greg Westrick, Vice President at RELEX Solutions. “The ability to automate routine planning activities while maintaining visibility across the network can have a meaningful impact on both operational efficiency and customer experience. We’re proud to support Best Buy Canada as they continue building a stronger foundation for planning and execution.”

2026 RTIH Innovation Awards

Forecasting and replenishment will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.

The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world.

Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.

Check out our 2025 winners here.

Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.

In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”

“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”

He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”

Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.

text:
Novo CEO Mike Doustdar told CNBC that the pharmaceutical giant is considering M&A opportunities as it faces growing competition in the crowded weight-loss market.

"Let's see where the gaps are, and let's go out and see who has produced or is about to introduce better drugs than we are able to do on our own, and when that gap can be filled with M&A, we are actually quite interested about it," Doustdar said on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.

He was speaking after the company faced investor pressure at its Capital Markets Day event on Monday, where it unveiled a turnaround plan that failed to convince markets it was ready to compete when the active ingredient in its weight-loss medication Wegovy starts losing key exclusivity in the early 2030s.

Novo was last seen trading just below the flatline, down 0.75%, after falling nearly 8% on Monday, its worst trading day since February.

"I think yesterday we laid out a more clear strategy of the direction we want to take the company at. We talked about diversification of the company, but yet the reaction tells me that there's still some work to do in convincing some of the investors," Doustdar said.

The company outlined plans to release over five "multi-blockbuster" drugs by 2030, which it expects to generate more than 150 billion Danish kroner ($23 billion) in sales by 2035. It also guided for revenue growth that is in line with industry peers such as Eli Lilly , AstraZeneca, Amgen, Biogen, Merck, AbbVie, and Novartis.

The plans disappointed investors who were hoping for a "miracle," especially as its target growth is in line with its peers, signalling slower progress than expected, analysts told CNBC on Monday.

Novo's key U.S. rival Eli Lilly has captured a large share of the weight loss market with its injectable GLP-1 drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound despite launching years after.

Lilly's CEO David Ricks told CNBC on Monday that a third of new GLP-1 patients are now taking its oral weight loss pill, Foundayo. "We're confident long term," he said.

While Novo's shares have declined 34% over the past year, Lilly is up just over 54% in the past 12 months.

Doustdar said the company plans to diversify beyond its core areas of diabetes and obesity, including building out its portfolio within blood and endocrine disorders, liver disease and cardiovascular disease.

"It is the right time now that I feel comfortable about the core to speak about the diversification of the company in adjacent areas that are not new to us either," he added.

"So it would be more obvious for me to imagine that we will be making more deals in areas outside of the core than in the core."

CNBC's Elsa Ohlen contributed to this report.

text:
Eli Lilly manufacturing race behind the pill race

Ricks was breaking ground on a $6.5 billion manufacturing facility at Generation Park that will produce Foundayo and the active ingredients for Lilly's small-molecule medicines across cardiology, oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. The plant is expected to be operational by 2030.

The Houston groundbreaking is one piece of a $27 billion commitment Lilly made in February 2025 to build four new U.S. facilities. Since 2020, the company has committed more than $50 billion to expanding its global manufacturing network.

Related: BofA points to the Eli Lilly market that could outsize the U.S.

Ricks has repeatedly framed that scale of capital commitment not just as a Trump-administration goodwill gesture but also as a genuine competitive moat against Novo Nordisk (NVO).

The production capacity race is critical because the oral pill market is now supply-constrained. Foundayo booked $98 million in sales in Q2 2026, its first full quarter on the market. But Ricks acknowledged that manufacturing scale is the binding constraint on how quickly the market can grow.

In the U.S., Lilly held a 60.9% share of the obesity and diabetes drug market in the second quarter, compared with Novo's 38.8%, according to Lilly's Q2 earnings presentation. With that, the Houston plant infrastructure makes the long-term dominance sustainable.

The bigger story: Medicare, access, and what finally changes for obesity treatment

The truly transformative development in this story is not Foundayo itself. It is Medicare coverage of obesity drugs, which began in July 2026, as mentioned.

For the first time, tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries have access to prescription weight-loss medications with insurance coverage. That policy shift expands the addressable patient population in ways the private insurance market alone never reached.

Oral medications like Foundayo are specifically positioned to benefit from broader access. Patients who were deterred by injectables, cost, or access barriers can now reach an oral option covered by the nation's largest public insurer.

Lilly's Q2 2026 total revenue of $23 billion grew 48% year over year, driven primarily by Mounjaro and Zepbound volume, according to the company's Q2 earnings release.

Foundayo's $98 million Q2 debut is a small number relative to that base. But the Houston plant that breaks ground today is being built for the version of this market that exists in 2030, when Medicare coverage has had three full years to pull previously untreated patients into the category.

Ricks said Lilly is confident in its long-term position in the oral pill segment. On performance, LLY has retraced to $1,164.89 from its all-time high of $1,292.65 reached on Aug. 19, but is still up 55.88% over the past year, according to Yahoo Finance.

LLY could outperform the broader market over the next 12 months, based on the latest analyst ratings. According to TheStreet, of the 22 analysts who rated the stock over the past three months, 20 recommend buying, one has a hold rating, and one recommends selling.

text:
Insider Brief

Microsoft opened a 15,000-square-foot quantum research center at the University of Maryland that will support hardware research, partner integration, workforce training and government collaboration.

The center will give DARPA on-site access to Microsoft’s latest topological quantum system, including qubits built on its Majorana 2 chip, for independent testing under the agency’s utility-scale quantum program.

Microsoft is also launching a quantum hardware makerspace, annual measurement-based computing workshops and UMD postdoctoral funding, with partners including AMD, Intel, IQM, Fermilab, Riverlane and Quantum Motion.

Microsoft has opened a quantum research center in Maryland that will house one of its topological quantum systems for independent testing by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, widening the government’s role in evaluating the company’s path toward large-scale quantum computers.

The 15,000-square-foot center, located in the University of Maryland’s Discovery District, combines Microsoft’s proprietary research space with laboratories for partner companies, a DARPA testing area and a hands-on training lab. Microsoft reports in a company blog post that the project was developed with the university, the state-backed Capital of Quantum Initiative and other industry partners.

The center gives DARPA on-site access to Microsoft’s latest topological quantum system, including qubits built on the company’s Majorana 2 chip, which based on an approach that has drawn close attention because it relies on an emerging class of quantum devices designed to be more error resistant.

DARPA will have full access to the system as part of its evaluation work under the Underexplored Systems for Utility-Scale Quantum Computing program, according to the post that was written by Dr. Charles Tahan, Partner, Microsoft Quantum. That program is part of DARPA’s broader Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, which seeks to determine whether competing quantum-computing approaches can produce commercially useful machines by 2033.

Microsoft is among the companies that have advanced to the final stage of the utility-scale program, according to the company. The evaluation effort also includes the Air Force Research Laboratory, Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory and national laboratories including Los Alamos, Oak Ridge, Lawrence Berkeley and Lawrence Livermore.

The Maryland center adds physical infrastructure to a partnership that Microsoft announced a year ago. With support from Maryland Gov. Wes Moore’s Capital of Quantum Initiative, the state acquired and renovated the Discovery Center, while Microsoft, UMD and the initiative designed the quantum facility within it.

Microsoft said the center will support research, partner integration, workforce training and government engagement. It will also provide space for future prototypes and for companies seeking to connect quantum hardware or components to Microsoft’s software platform.

A Test for Topological Qubits

Microsoft’s system uses topological qubits, an approach intended to reduce the burden of quantum error correction. Quantum computers are highly sensitive to environmental noise and operational imperfections, meaning useful systems will need to detect and correct errors repeatedly while calculations are underway.

The company introduced Majorana 2 as its second-generation topological quantum chip. Microsoft said the chip uses a new material stack that replaces aluminum with lead, a change it said improves performance. The system has drawn criticism from some in the scientific community who were skeptical of the claims.

However, the delivery to DARPA may help address those criticisms by opening the company’s hardware to an outside testing team with expertise across hardware, control systems, software and applications. Microsoft said independent access is a necessary step in assessing whether its approach can lead to an economically relevant quantum computer.

The company has described its goal as building systems capable of handling useful workloads beyond the reach of conventional computers. That remains challenging as quantum processors have advanced rapidly in recent years, but the field has yet to demonstrate a broadly useful, fault-tolerant machine that can consistently outperform classical systems on commercially important work.

Microsoft’s Maryland facility will also serve as a location where prospective partners can test how their technologies work with the company’s broader quantum platform. Hardware builders could use the space to integrate machines or components, while developers and end users could explore potential applications, Microsoft said.

The company’s strategy is built around supporting multiple quantum hardware types through a common software and infrastructure layer, rather than tying its platform solely to its own topological-qubit program.

Training With Hardware

A central feature of the new center will be a quantum hardware makerspace intended to give students, researchers, educators and people transitioning from other technical fields a chance to work directly with equipment.

Microsoft said initial partners include AMD, Bluefors, Intel, IQM, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Riverlane and Quantum Motion. Their contributions are expected to provide access to hardware as well as technical expertise.

The company said the program differs from quantum education efforts centered mainly on theory or software. Instead, participants will be expected to work through practical problems across the quantum hardware stack, including selecting designs, deciding what to measure and diagnosing unexpected experimental results.

Microsoft is also working with Fermilab to expand the use of quantum-control technologies across hardware platforms. With UMD, the partners are exploring how Fermilab’s Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit, known as QICK, could be used in education.

The effort reflects a growing industry concern that quantum computing will require a larger workforce able to work across physics, engineering, electronics, controls and software. Many quantum systems depend on specialized equipment, including cryogenic hardware, lasers, control electronics and complex calibration routines.

Microsoft said it hopes the Maryland makerspace will become a model that can be expanded more broadly as lessons and course material emerge from the program.

Measurement-Based Computing Focus

The center will also support research in measurement-based quantum computing, an approach in which measurement results help determine subsequent operations in a quantum calculation.

Microsoft said it plans to launch an annual workshop series focused on improving the speed and accuracy of measurements, developing error-correcting codes and advancing verification and validation methods. The company is also funding its first quantum postdoctoral positions at UMD in research areas of mutual interest to Microsoft and university faculty.

Fast, accurate measurements are particularly important in error-corrected quantum computers because the system must identify errors and decide how to respond quickly enough to prevent them from spreading through a calculation.

Microsoft said its Azure-based quantum platform includes developer tools, a real-time operating system for quantum computers and support for different qubit technologies. It also pointed to its work with Atom Computing, which is applying Microsoft’s error-correction technology to neutral-atom hardware.

The companies are developing a machine called Magne, planned to have 50 logical qubits and scheduled for operation at QuNorth in Denmark by early 2027, Microsoft said. Logical qubits are groups of physical qubits combined through error correction to produce a more stable computational unit.

Anthropic debuted Claude Opus 5.5, which it says performs at the level of its flagship Fable 5.1 model but costs around 40% less to run than Opus 5, which came out in July. It’s the first release in a new family of models, with Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 expected “over the coming weeks,” Anthropic said.

Anthropic said the model is its most efficient, and it’s “passing these efficiency savings on to our customers in the form of price cuts and rate limit increases.”

OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, offshoots of its flagship GPT-6 Astra model that came out earlier this month. The idea is to offer a version of Astra for everyday work, OpenAI said. It also slashed the API cost by 50% lower than the pricing on a promotion it’s currently running for Astra’s predecessor, GPT-5.6. OpenAI often releases lower priced versions of its flagship models, as it did with GPT-5.6.

OpenAI’s release offers lower API pricing than Anthropic’s, based on each company’s announcement, as shown in the table below. OpenAI attributes the cost reductions to “improvements in caching and inference,” and, like Anthropic, says it’s also “passing those savings directly onto users and customers.”

The two labs are already deep into an all-out price war—something that could put pressure on their ability to profit from their models down the line.

“OpenAI and Anthropic are engaged in a price war that is driving down the price of AI and therefore driving down their ability to profit from it and grow the price of models,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, told Fortune.

The battle is playing out on two fronts, Kharazian said: the labs are rolling out cheaper models that businesses are shifting toward, such as Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol and Luna, while also announcing outright price cuts on their most expensive ones.

That dynamic is how technology markets have traditionally worked, he said, but it’s something that more bullish investors may not be factoring in.

“AI bulls assume that there will be highly performant models that provide more and more value, and therefore they should be more expensive,” Kharazian said. “But that is not how normal technology makes it to market.”

An AI slowdown?

These are the first model releases since both companies publicly called for a coordinated attempt to “pace the frontier,” or slow the development of the most advanced models. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post laying out his plan for a slowdown in mid-September, which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman supported in an X post—a rare moment of solidarity between the two.

Anthropic acknowledged that the release of Opus 5.5 is its first since Amodei’s call to “pace the frontier.” The company said that Opus 5.5 underwent the company’s most rigorous alignment testing to date and was evaluated by outside groups. The model also is also launching with the same tier of cybersecurity, biology, and frontier-AI-development safeguards previously reserved for the company’s more advanced model Fable 5.1.

While today’s releases from both companies are not frontier models, as in they are not a major step up in capabilities, they show that both companies continue to push AI capabilities forward outside of the frontier. The real fight for the future of their businesses could be in gaining everyday business customers, not necessarily offering the most powerful (and expensive) models possible.

Many businesses are tightening their AI wallets and applying more scrutiny to the ROI of the technology, Randall Hunt, CTO at the AI consulting company Caylent, said.

“CFOs have seen some of the sticker shock, and they haven’t seen some of the gains that were promised in the initial investments,” Hunt said. “So they’re coming back to their planning for 2027 and beyond, and saying, ‘How can we optimize our costs here?’”

title: NVIDIA, Google Launch Alliance to Speed Data Center Connections
description:
Emerald AI, Google and NVIDIA launched the AI Energy Management Alliance to accelerate flexible AI data center connections, improve grid reliability and address electricity constraints through measurable demand management.
To attend this need, Emerald AI, Google and NVIDIA announced the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), a coalition designed to advance data centers capable of dynamically managing their electricity consumption.
AI Data Centers Face Growing Power Constraints Electricity availability has become a critical factor in the expansion of AI infrastructure across the United States.
AI data centers introduce additional complexity.
Google contributes experience with flexible electricity demand, reporting more than one gigawatt of demand flexibility covered by agreements with US utilities.
text:
Emerald AI, Google and NVIDIA launched the AI Energy Management Alliance to accelerate flexible AI data center connections, improve grid reliability and address electricity constraints through measurable demand management.

AI infrastructure is in a phase in which access to electricity may determine how quickly computing capacity can expand. As data centers place greater demands on power grids, technology companies and energy providers are exploring ways to make electricity consumption more responsive to grid conditions.

To attend this need, Emerald AI, Google and NVIDIA announced the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), a coalition designed to advance data centers capable of dynamically managing their electricity consumption.

The initiative brings together companies across the AI and energy value chains, including infrastructure providers, utilities, power producers and regional grid operators.

Its objective is to establish performance-based frameworks that enable faster interconnections while maintaining grid reliability and addressing electricity affordability.

“The rules governing power for AI are being written now,” reads NVIDIA’s announcement, emphasizing the need for common frameworks for performance, reliability and collaboration.

The alliance reflects a broader shift in how the industry approaches AI infrastructure. Instead of treating data centers solely as large, continuous electricity consumers, AEMA proposes recognizing certain facilities as controllable resources capable of adjusting their demand when the grid requires support.

AI Data Centers Face Growing Power Constraints

Electricity availability has become a critical factor in the expansion of AI infrastructure across the United States. Conventional interconnection processes generally evaluate large facilities according to their expected electricity requirements, often assuming that demand remains relatively stable.

AI data centers introduce additional complexity. Computing workloads can vary in urgency, duration and location, creating opportunities to adjust electricity consumption without interrupting every service operating within a facility.

Flexible data centers can respond to grid conditions through several mechanisms, including shifting computing workloads, discharging battery storage, using paired generation or reducing demand during system contingencies.

The potential benefit extends beyond individual facilities. By managing electricity consumption during periods of grid stress, data centers could make more efficient use of existing capacity and reduce the need for certain infrastructure upgrades.

For utilities and grid operators, however, the value of flexibility depends on whether promised reductions can be delivered consistently. A facility that offers flexibility must demonstrate how quickly it can respond, how long it can maintain a reduction and how it will behave during an emergency.

AEMA therefore advocates for technology-neutral, performance-based requirements. Rather than prescribing a specific hardware or software solution, the alliance focuses on measurable outcomes such as response speed, duration, predictability and emergency performance.

This approach could allow facilities to combine different technologies according to their operational requirements. Workload orchestration, batteries, local generation and other energy resources may all contribute to meeting the same performance standards.

From Interconnection Rules to Operational Commitments

The alliance proposes several principles for integrating flexibility into the interconnection process.

These include defining ride-through, curtailment and contingency-response obligations before a facility connects to the grid. The framework also calls for standardized technical requirements, performance metrics and operational data sharing.

Another priority is establishing faster, risk-adjusted interconnection pathways for customers that make credible and verifiable flexibility commitments.

Cost allocation represents a further component. AEMA proposes that interconnection costs reflect the actual impacts and benefits of a facility, including potentially avoided upgrades and improved ramping capabilities.

The distinction between firm and flexible demand is central to this model. A data center may still require continuous electricity for critical services, but other workloads could be shifted or reduced under defined conditions.

Training processes, batch computing and selected inference workloads may offer scheduling flexibility, while latency-sensitive applications and critical customer services could require uninterrupted operation.

The challenge is translating these differences into enforceable agreements. Utilities need clear information about a facility’s maximum firm demand, response times, reduction capacity and recovery behavior.

Uncontrolled recovery also presents a potential risk. If delayed workloads restart simultaneously after a reduction event, the resulting increase in electricity consumption could create a new demand peak.

Consequently, the alliance’s proposed framework extends beyond reducing electricity use. It seeks to establish how facilities should operate before, during and after grid disruptions.

Implications for Mexico’s Data Center Expansion

Although AEMA is focused on the US energy system, its approach has relevance for Mexico, where data center expansion is also confronting electricity availability, transmission capacity and operational requirements.

MBN previously reported that energy delivery represents a central constraint for new data center developments. Industry executives have highlighted the need to coordinate utilities, developers, equipment providers and public authorities as computing facilities require greater power density and cooling capacity.

The challenge is particularly relevant as investment expands beyond established data center hubs. Projects in Guanajuato and Mexico City demonstrate how digital infrastructure development is becoming connected to industrial activity, proximity to users and supporting electricity infrastructure.

In this context, flexible energy management could provide an additional mechanism for evaluating how large computing facilities interact with local networks. Its applicability, however, would depend on Mexico’s regulatory framework, grid characteristics and the technical capabilities of participating operators.

AEMA’s technology-neutral approach also leaves room for different combinations of generation, storage and workload management. This could be relevant to markets where transmission expansion and electricity delivery timelines influence investment decisions.

The alliance does not eliminate the need for substations, transmission infrastructure or reliable power generation. Instead, it proposes that a facility’s ability to manage its demand should become part of how its connection is evaluated.

Emerald AI and NVIDIA have already collaborated with energy and infrastructure companies on AI facilities designed to respond to grid conditions in real time. AEMA seeks to broaden these efforts by connecting technology, energy and policy stakeholders around deployable models.

Google contributes experience with flexible electricity demand, reporting more than one gigawatt of demand flexibility covered by agreements with US utilities.

These existing efforts provide an operational foundation, but scaling flexibility from individual demonstrations to large commercial campuses presents additional challenges.

text:
Sept 22 (Reuters) - Microsoft will consider shareholder proposals at its annual meetings through next year, at the request of an activist looking to preserve investor rights as they come under pressure from a contentious U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission rule change proposed last week.

Under an agreement with conservative activist Paul Chesser, seen by Reuters, Microsoft will continue to apply existing thresholds for investors to submit resolutions for a vote, even as the SEC considers changes that critics say would sideline individual investors, religious groups, unions and others who have had a say through the shareholder proposal process for decades.

The agreement only lasts a year, but could effectively offset efforts by the regulatory agency to shift power away from investors to corporate executives. Chesser said he hopes Microsoft's approach will become a corporate-governance model to assure mom-and-pop investors a voice that can be followed by other companies.

"Microsoft put in writing that the smallest long-term owners of the company will still have a way to be heard next year, no matter what the SEC does," said Chesser, director at the National Legal and Policy Center. "Every other company that claims to value its shareholders should be asked why it won't do the same," he said.

In an e-mailed statement, a Microsoft spokesperson said: "With the Securities and Exchange Commission announcing that its shareholder proposal regulatory framework is under review, we agreed to maintain the current eligibility thresholds for one year, providing Microsoft and its shareholders a clear and predictable process for the next proxy cycle."

Shareholder resolutions on topics like climate change, workforce diversity and executive pay have become the focus of many shareholder meetings in recent years, although many have received diminishing support from major fund firms.

EARLY EXAMPLE

Microsoft's meeting is set for December 8 and traditionally has been held early in the proxy cycle that runs through June 30 of each year, bringing attention to the company's governance procedures.

Last week SEC Chair Paul Atkins, an appointee of US President Donald Trump, proposed to end the agency's oversight of the resolutions process and move the function to state officials, which activists saw as a shift that would diminish their influence. The move is part of a broader shift of power away from investors toward managers by the Republican-dominated commission.

The agreement between Chesser and Microsoft, seen by Reuters, says Microsoft will continue to apply previous eligibility requirements for investors to submit resolutions for a vote. Chesser's group has similar resolutions pending with Procter & Gamble and Oracle and may submit more.

P&G's annual meeting is set for October 13. In its proxy statement dated August 28, the company recommended votes against the proposal, among other things calling it premature since the SEC hadn't yet proposed its rulemaking. A P&G representative declined to comment.

Oracle's AGM has not yet been set. A representative did not immediately respond to questions.

text:
Fashion's renewable-energy transition has a coordination problem.

Levi Strauss & Co. and Marks & Spencer are joining forces on a supplier program designed to pool brands' engagement efforts and help manufacturers navigate energy markets, procurement options and implementation.

More from WWD

Oxford Report Puts Fashion's Farmland 'Influence' at 30 Percent

London Fashion Week Revs Up With a Lineup of New Brands and Some Old Favorites

Adidas and an NYC Sneaker Boutique Made a Cannoli-themed Samba Just in Time for San Gennaro

Unveiled Tuesday during Climate Week NYC, the Fashion Renewable Collaborative, or FRC, will offer participating suppliers digital education, market guidance and support in assessing and procuring renewable electricity. Schneider Electric's SE Advisory Services will serve as the initiative's global implementation partner.

The founding companies are inviting other fashion brands to join as sponsors or members.

Unlike programs centered primarily on setting targets or publishing roadmaps, the FRC is intended to help suppliers pursue energy purchases and installations. Its menu includes power purchase agreements, energy attribute certificates, on-site and distributed renewable generation and energy storage.

The companies did not disclose an initial supplier count, geographic scope, funding commitment or renewable-electricity procurement target.

The initiative takes aim at one of fashion's most persistent climate problems: Brands have set emissions targets covering supply chains they do not own, while the mills, dye houses and factories expected to deliver those reductions face varying customer demands and sharply different renewable-energy markets.

The potential payoff is substantial. Textile processing—including the mills and dye houses that consume large amounts of heat and electricity—generates more than half of apparel's emissions, according to the Apparel Impact Institute. In a roadmap produced with the World Resources Institute, renewable electricity accounted for roughly two-thirds of the sector's potential emissions cuts.

But suppliers cannot simply choose clean power from a menu. What is available—and at what price—depends on the market. Some options require specialized knowledge, enough demand to make a deal viable and commitments that can stretch over several years. The difficulty only compounds when the same factory is answering to multiple brands with different requests and reporting requirements.

The collaborative is meant to reduce some of that complexity—and the duplication created when multiple brands separately approach the same manufacturer.

"It's become abundantly clear that the most effective way forward on emissions reduction is working in partnership with suppliers," Jennifer DuBuisson, Levi Strauss & Co.'s senior director of sustainability, said. "The Fashion Renewable Collaborative enables greater support of suppliers that want to access or would like to increase use of renewable electricity but haven't been able to so far, helping facilitate adoption while reducing unnecessary duplication."

The FRC builds on supplier programs already operated by Levi's and M&S. Together, those efforts registered nearly 500 supplier facilities, according to the companies. They did not disclose how many of those facilities subsequently procured renewable electricity, installed generation capacity or reduced their emissions through the programs.

For M&S, the FRC builds on Re, its existing supplier-decarbonization program. The retailer has pledged to reach net-zero emissions across its value chain by 2040 under its wider Plan A strategy.

Katharine Beacham, M&S's head of sustainability and materials in fashion, home and beauty, said the collaboration would provide suppliers with "practical support, resources and greater access to renewable electricity."

Participating suppliers will use Schneider Electric's Resource Advisor+ for Supply Chain platform for onboarding, education, readiness assessments and progress tracking. The consultancy said it manages more than 20 active supply-chain decarbonization initiatives involving upward of 3,100 supplier companies, including 16 renewable-energy cohorts involving multiple buyers.

The technology is meant to create a common experience for brands and manufacturers while guiding suppliers from education to procurement. The program's impact, however, will ultimately depend on how many suppliers move beyond registration and reviews to secure renewable power.

text:
Microsoft said Tuesday that it led an industry-wide disruption of a subscription-based scam platform that used an AI chatbot to compromise 12,000 Microsoft accounts over a few-month span.

Named EvilTokens, the platform was introduced over a Telegram channel in February and charged an initial $1,500 fee and a recurring $500 charge each month after that. EvilTokens provided a single service for streamlining most steps required to compromise email accounts in large numbers. From there, the platform helped customers analyze inboxes, select targets that would provide the biggest potential payouts, and draft follow-up emails that provided realistic ruses for tricking company employees into transferring funds to attacker-controlled accounts.

Minutes, not days

“While EvilTokens helped cybercriminals access email accounts, at the center of the service was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim’s inbox and help criminals identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities, as well as other circumstances where fraud was most likely to succeed,” Microsoft said. “The platform could even recommend fraud strategies, including drafting messages that impersonated trusted contacts to help criminals trick victims into taking action.”

Microsoft said users of EvilToken compromised 12,000 customer accounts belonging to 10,000 organizations around the world, with the highest concentration of them located in the US. Countries with the next-largest numbers were Canada, the UK, Australia, India, and France. Victim organizations included wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education, and healthcare. SpyCloud, a security firm that assisted in the disruption operation, has more details about victims here.

Using a legal process and a network of partners, Microsoft seized 50 websites and 150 more domains used to operate EvilTokens. The UK’s Metropolitan Police Service arrested two men on suspicion of offenses allegedly connected to the crime platform.

Account compromises were achieved through a legitimate OAuth process known as device code authentication. This form of authentication is designed for TVs and input-constrained devices, meaning those that lack the interface for performing normal log-in processes. In this model, the device being signed into presents a code and instructs the user to enter it into a browser on a separate device. The new device is then authenticated.

EvilTokens provided customers with a platform that automated the sending of large numbers of spam. Users who clicked on malicious links or attachments in the emails were directed to a webpage running a hidden automation script that interacts with the user’s Microsoft identity provider in real time to generate a code for enrolling a device belonging to the attacker. SpyCloud identified the ID provider as Microsoft Entra.

The user would then see the device code along with instructions to copy it and enter it into the official Microsoft device login portal. Complex backend logic (Node.js) in the platform allowed the operation to bypass traditional signature- or pattern-based detection. The technique allowed the process to work end to end, from the generation of dynamic device codes to post-compromise activities. Microsoft has more on the abuse of the OAuth process here.

A dashboard allowed users to tailor lures to the profiles of the organizations they targeted. The platform largely automated the rest of the attack process as well. EvilTokens analyzed 5,000 compromised emails at a time. Using AI, the platform identified employees authorized to disburse large sums of money, the managers these employees reported to, and convincing scenarios under which the manager or others could persuade the employees to transfer money into what turned out to be attacker-controlled accounts.

Microsoft said that EvilTokens represents a major shift in the mass compromise and post-compromise of accounts. Normally, it took time for attackers to sift through thousands of emails to assemble the organization’s management chart, suppliers, customers, and other relationships with third parties. That burden is greatly reduced with AI-assisted tools.

“For organizations, the lesson is: assume that once an inbox is compromised, criminals may understand its contents in minutes, not days,” Microsoft said. “Strong identity protections and monitoring remain essential, but organizations should also independently verify requests to change payment information, redirect funds, or approve unusual transactions through a trusted second channel.”

text:
Anthropic and OpenAI on Tuesday each announced new, less costly artificial intelligence models as both frontier labs continue to face stiff competition from cheaper, open-weight competitors.

OpenAI introduced additional tiers to its GPT-6 family, with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, slashing the API prices by 50% compared with GPT-5.6 promotional pricing.

Sol, which is a tier below Astra, is meant for more complex workloads like coding, while the company's Luna offering is geared toward "high-volume tasks" such as extracting information or summarizing documents, the company wrote.

Anthropic unveiled Claude Opus 5.5 on Tuesday, its latest release in the new Claude 5.5 model family. The company described the latest release as a more token-efficient version that will cost around 40% less to run than the company's Opus 5.

"One of the things we're continuing to innovate on is how to make that thinking, how to make the answering more efficient, so it uses less tokens depending on your effort setting," Dianne Penn, head of product management, research and labs at Anthropic, told CNBC in an interview.

The separate releases are the first to roll out since Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for an industrywide slowdown on developing advanced AI as the debate about model safety reached a fever pitch in recent weeks.

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon set off the debate when he posted to X on Sept. 8 that he had quit his job, warning that both labs were "gambling with our lives."

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk also joined Amodei's call.

The new releases come as OpenAI and Anthropic work to satisfy customers who are looking for more cost-effective models and seeking to rein in AI spending.

The labs are facing pressure from companies offering cheaper, open-weight models, including Chinese firms Alibaba, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek

Eli Lilly broke ground Monday on a $6.5B facility at Generation Park in Northeast Houston, according to Bisnow.

The plant will produce the pharmaceutical giant's newly approved GLP-1 pill Foundayo along with other small-molecule medicines and advanced therapeutics. Gov. Greg Abbott called it the largest active pharmaceutical ingredient project in Texas history.

A Decade in the Making

McCord Development broke ground on Generation Park 13 years ago. The move laid the foundation for large-scale biotech and life sciences tenants.

The 4,300-acre master-planned site later became a focus for life sciences investment. After losing Amgen's $550M biomanufacturing project in 2021, McCord doubled down on education and workforce training.

Meanwhile, Lilly first announced its Houston investment about a year ago. Monday's groundbreaking now delivers on that commitment.

The Details

The facility will manufacture Foundayo, a synthetic oral GLP-1 medicine. The FDA approved it on April 1 for weight management.

The plant will also produce other small-molecule medicines and advanced therapeutics. Meanwhile, Lilly is studying Foundayo for other potential uses.

Those include Type 2 diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea.

The project is expected to create more than 600 high-wage jobs. In addition, Lilly is contributing $12.5M to San Jacinto College.

The funding will help build training pathways into advanced chemical synthesis manufacturing careers. Lilly will also donate another $2.5M to the college's foundation for student scholarships.

Zooming Out

The Houston plant is Lilly's fifth domestic active pharmaceutical ingredient production site announced since 2020. It is part of the company's broader $50B push to reshore U.S. medicine manufacturing.
